newsitem.title: UK: BOE TO WARN OF UPSIDE RISKS IN INFLATION REPORT.
newsitem.headline: BOE TO WARN OF UPSIDE RISKS IN INFLATION REPORT.

text.p: The Bank of England looks set to flesh out its new sanguine outlook for British inflation and interest rates in the quarterly inflation report on Wednesday, but analysts said it will also issue a clear warning of the numerous upside risks.
"The Bank has to maintain a reasonable level of consistency with the upbeat statement it made last week in order to retain credibility," said Mark Miller, UK economist at Morgan Stanley.
"But given the weight of evidence of strong consumer demand and activity I think the Bank's views will be phrased to highlight the risks to policy at this stage of the cycle."
The Bank is due to publish its quarterly inflation report on Wednesday at 0930 GMT.

But, in a statement accompanying the quarter point rate rise last Thursday, the central bank pre-empted the report and hinted it believed underlying inflation was on track to hit the government's 2.5 percent target and that rates may stay on hold for the time being.
"Upward pressures on the exchange rate should be reduced by the perception that interest rates have reached a level consistent with the inflation target," it said.
This first attempt to talk down the pound met with stunning success and sterling lost 12 pfennigs in response, although it partly recovered this week.

Economists said in keeping with the statement, the Bank's central forecast will show underlying inflation hitting the government's 2.5 percent target in two years time. The Bank's forecast is made for the current level of interest rates.
Latest figures released on Tuesday showed the targeted inflation rate edged up to 3.0 percent in July from 2.7 percent in June.
David Mackie, UK economist at JP Morgan, thought the Bank would not depart too much from last week's message.

"The Bank will tell us again that on the basis of its current forecasts for growth and the exchange rate, it thinks interest rates at seven percent are enough for inflation to hit the target," said David Mackie, UK economist at JP Morgan.
But that, he said, was very different from saying interest rates would stay at seven percent, the conclusion some traders and analysts reached last week.

"Mervyn King will choose his words carefully and make it clear that on the basis of the Bank's current view of the economy, rates at seven percent are high enough. And he may say the risks for inflation are more on the upside," said Mackie.
The Bank's chief economist is due to hold a news briefing at 0930 GMT, immediately after the release of the report.
And economists will be eager to see what assumptions the Bank is making about growth and the exchange rate.
In the July 2 budget, the government forecast growth slowing dramatically next year to 2.5 percent growth from 3.25 percent this year.
While the Bank will not make its GDP forecast public, it will allude to it in its analysis of consumption and investment.
"I think the Bank will make it clear it also assumes some sort of slowdown later this year," said Mackie.
And in terms of the exchange rate, the Bank will project the path of sterling using interest rate differentials between the UK and overseas.
In the May report, the Bank hinted that it expected some of the recent appreciation to be reversed.

"And in last week's statement the Bank referred to a perception in the market that rates had peaked which would help to take the pressure off the pound. We must assume since there was no such perception at the time. the Bank must believe that itself," said Miller.
But if the Bank overdoes it in talking up the dangers to its benign inflation forecast, it risks undoing all the good work last week on talking down the pound.

"Last week the pound fell purely because the market thought we may be nearing the peak in interest rates," said one trader. "If the Bank now suggests that this may not actually be the case, sterling will continue to recover from that fall."
The pound stood at 2.9460/70 marks on Tuesday compared with a low of 2.91 marks made after the Bank's statement.
